name: Checkli
tagline: Build reusable checklists from templates, run them repeatedly, share or print the results.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is checklists with templates on top: users, templates, instances, items, checkbox state. There is no algorithm, no model, no third party API doing the heavy lifting, and nothing that needs anyone else to be on the platform for your copy to work. An agent can produce a local version with template duplication, ordered items, progress tracking, print styling and JSON export in one sitting. What you do not get is the public template gallery, which is the part of Checkli that actually took time to accumulate. If you mostly re-run your own five recurring checklists, that gallery was never the reason you were there.
coreLoopDIY: Create a checklist template once, spawn a dated run from it whenever you need it, tick items off, and keep the completed runs as a history you can print or export.
requirements: Node 20 and a machine to run it on
Optional: a cheap VPS or Fly.io box if you want it reachable from your phone
whatYouLose: The public template library, thousands of prewritten checklists you can fork instead of writing
Share links that render nicely for people who do not have your app
Print and PDF layouts somebody already fussed over
Any team or client-facing polish: logos on exported checklists, collaborator assignment
moatNotes: The template gallery is accumulated content, not technology. It is a real reason to visit and a bad reason to pay if you only use your own checklists.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because writing checklists is the annoying part, not storing them. Checkli's value for most paying users is forking a decent prewritten template for onboarding or cleaning or SEO audits, branding it, and handing it to a contractor or client who is never going to install anything. A local build serves the person who already knows what their checklist says and just wants it to come back clean and empty every Monday, which is a smaller but very real slice of the user base.
notes: The easiest kind of yes: the data model fits on an index card and nothing about it needs the internet.
prompt:
Build a local-first reusable checklist app called Checklist Runner.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Drizzle ORM for schema and migrations. Single user, no auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no external API calls. Database file at ./data/app.db, created on first run.

Schema:
- templates: id, title, description, createdAt, updatedAt
- template_items: id, templateId, position, text, note (nullable)
- runs: id, templateId (nullable if template deleted), title snapshot, startedAt, completedAt (nullable)
- run_items: id, runId, position, text, note, checkedAt (nullable)

Behaviour:
- Templates list page: create, rename, duplicate, delete, reorder items by drag or by up/down buttons, inline add item.
- Starting a run copies the template items into run_items so later template edits never mutate history.
- Run page: checkboxes with optimistic UI, a progress bar, per-item notes, mark run complete when all items are checked or manually.
- History page: runs grouped by template, filter by completed or in progress, reopen a completed run.
- Print stylesheet: a run prints as a clean one-column sheet with title, date and empty or filled boxes. No nav, no buttons.
- Export: download all templates and runs as JSON, and import that same JSON back. Also export a single run as Markdown.
- Seed three example templates on first boot so the app is not empty.

In scope: everything above, keyboard shortcuts for check next item, dark mode via system preference.
Out of scope: multi-user, sharing links, a public template gallery, email, mobile apps, file uploads, integrations.

Use server actions for mutations, no separate REST layer. Any config goes in .env with a committed .env.example; there should be almost nothing in it. Ship a README with one install command, one dev command, one build command, and a note on backing up data/app.db by copying the file.
